newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Portugal tobacco selloff closely fought race.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Portugal tobacco selloff closely fought race.

text.p: The imminent privatisation of Portugal's main cigarette manufacturer, Tabaqueira, is a political hot potato pitting the Spanish tobacco industry against U.S. giant Philip Morris and French group Seita.
Analysts said the race was too close to call as the government prepared to give its final decision, perhaps next week, even though Philip Morris appeared best-placed to win.

A special jury presiding over the privatisation ranked Philip Morris, in alliance with Portugal's Jorge de Mello group, first among the bidders even though it did not offer the highest price, officials said.
Philip Morris offered 5,100 escudos per share for the 65 percent stake that the government is offering, which would bring in 33.15 billion escudos ($217 million) to state coffers.

Leading Spanish tobacco company Tabacalera, which is 52 percent state-owned, allied to Madeira company Empresa Madeirense de Tabacos, offered a higher price -- 5,610 escudos -- while French firm Seita bid 4,800 escudos.
But beside the price, the jury took into account the industrial plans that each candidate presented for Tabaqueira, which controls around 70 percent of the Portuguese market.
The government is not bound to implement the jury's opinion.
"The priority for the final decision has to be job creation and protection," said Mark Howard, equities analyst with Lloyds Bank Fund Managers in Cascais near Lisbon.

The bid by Philip Morris foresees the creation of 100 jobs, a new shift at Tabaqueira's factory at Albarraque near Lisbon and a hike in annual production to 21 billion cigarettes by 2001 from 10 billion now, a source linked to the bid said.
The production increase would bring in additional revenues to the government from cigarette taxes.

Analysts said Philip Morris's partnership with the Jorge de Mello group was significant as the Portuguese group already held 51 percent of loss-making food company Nutrinveste, a major employer. Tabaqueira owns the other 49 percent.
"If the Jorge de Mello group took over Nutrinveste completely, it could solve one headache for the government," said one Lisbon-based analyst, who asked not to be identified.
Discussions on the privatisation of Tabaqueira among officials at a meeting of the Portuguese and Spanish prime ministers in the Azores this week had turned up the political heat, analysts said.
A Finance Ministry source said that no decisions were taken at the meeting but the government could decide next week who had been designated to buy Tabaqueira.

Spain's Tabacalera turned up the pressure when it said this week that if it was chosen to take a majority stake in Tabaqueira, it would buy the remainder of the firm before the current deadline of two years, analysts said.

They said Tabacalera was anxious to win because it feared that if Philip Morris were chosen, its present deal to manufacture Philip Morris brands in Spain could be under threat as the U.S. firm moved its southern European centre to Portugal.
Tabacalera produces Philip Morris brands Marlboro and L&M in Spain under licence.

If Philip Morris won, it would control more than 90 percent of the Portuguese market. One press report said some international cigarette manufacturers would consider going to court if they believed it would break European Union anti-trust laws.
The Tabaqueira selloff is part of a Portuguese government privatisation programme that could bring in at least $450 million this year and a similar sum in 1997.
